description: NUML Software Engineering student crew leveraging advanced AI tools to build a futuristic Lunar Dashboard for mapping NASA's CLPS Moon landing sites.
summary:
LUNARIS is a web tool for planning around the Moon's south pole. A user picks a landing site and a date, and the app shows when the Sun is above the real terrain horizon, when Earth is geometrically in view, and how both change across a lunar day. Users can compare up to three scenarios, scan dates, view elevation, slope and hillshade layers, check simple requirements and print a one-page report.

It answers the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge by putting sunlight, Earth visibility and terrain in one place, using NASA data: SPICE and Horizons for positions, and LRO LOLA for topography.

It matters because planners today combine several tools by hand. LUNARIS labels every number with its source and shows missing data as unavailable instead of guessing, so the results can be trusted and checked.
details:
Live app: https://lunaris-ecru.vercel.app

Source code: https://github.com/MTFEnterprises/lunaris

What it does

LUNARIS lets a mission planner choose a site near the lunar south pole and a date, then shows how much sunlight the site gets and when Earth is in view. Sky View plots the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon. Timeline shows sunlit and Earth-visible periods across a lunar day. Compare puts up to three scenarios side by side and includes a date scan. Map and terrain shows elevation, slope and hillshade layers. Requirements checks a site against simple limits and answers pass, fail or unknown. Report gives a one-page summary with sources and limits.

How it works

Heavy calculations run offline. We computed Sun and Earth positions in the Moon body-fixed frame from NASA NAIF SPICE and JPL Horizons data, in 30-minute steps through January 2028. We built a 360-degree terrain horizon for each site from LRO LOLA topography at 80 m per pixel. The results are stored as small JSON and PNG files in the repository. A FastAPI backend written in Python with NumPy serves 14 endpoints, and a React web app shows the results. Backend and frontend are hosted together on Vercel.

What makes it different

Every response carries a provenance label: observed, published, calculated, estimated, illustrative or unavailable. When we cannot support a value, the app shows UNAVAILABLE and the reason, and never invents a number. Geometric and terrain-corrected results are kept separate. "Earth visible" is described only as a geometric communication opportunity, not a working radio link. A requirement with missing data returns unknown, never pass.

Limits

LUNARIS is a preliminary decision-support prototype. It is not flight-certified and not a NASA product. Thermal modelling is future work, and the API reports it as unavailable. Custom map points receive geometric results only, without terrain correction.

Tools

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, three.js, Vercel, GitHub. NASA data: LRO LOLA, NAIF SPICE, JPL Horizons and the LROC WAC mosaic.

Use of AI

We used Claude (Anthropic) and GitHub Copilot as coding and writing assistants. They helped us write and review code and tests, write documentation, and prepare the presentation slides. The team chose the design and the honesty rules, set the requirements, checked the results and reviewed all AI-assisted work. No images in the project are AI-generated; the Moon image comes from NASA's LROC.

Team

Five students from MTF Science Labs, Faisalabad, Pakistan, working on backend and platform, the science engine, terrain and geospatial data, the frontend, and visualization and content.
